name: Citrulline malate

lead: Citrulline malate combines L-citrulline with malic acid and is a common pre-workout ingredient. Users take it for a muscle pump, fuller-looking muscles, endurance in resistance sets and less soreness.

Citrulline is converted to arginine in the kidney, raising nitric oxide production and widening blood vessels, so more blood reaches working muscle. Meta-analyses report a small improvement in repetitions to failure with low certainty, and single trials often show no effect. No study in the sources reviewed has shown it increases muscle size.

paras: It is taken as a powder in pre-workout drinks before training, sometimes paired with tadalafil for blood flow. Pump effects are noticed within sessions.

It is legal and generally well tolerated; the main complaint is stomach upset at larger amounts. It can lower blood pressure slightly, which matters for people taking antihypertensive or erectile dysfunction drugs.

chain: Boosts nitric oxide and blood flow
angle.text: Citrulline malate raises nitric oxide and blood flow for a bigger pump and a few more reps, giving more training stimulus and a fuller look in the gym. Studies on reps and endurance are mixed, and effects on long-term muscle growth have not been shown.

lead: Citrulline malate (CM) is a supplement that combines the amino acid L-citrulline with malic acid. Citrulline is a non-essential alpha-amino acid and a key intermediate in the urea cycle, the pathway mammals use to convert ammonia to urea; it is also a byproduct of nitric oxide production from arginine [1]. Its name comes from citrullus, the Latin word for watermelon, from which it was first isolated in 1914 [1].

CM is a common ingredient in pre-workout powders, where it is promoted for muscle 'pump', blood flow, endurance in resistance sets and recovery [2][3]. The proposed mechanism is increased nitric oxide and blood flow to active muscle, with possible effects on ammonia handling and on ATP production through malate [2].

Published evidence on exercise performance is described by reviewers as equivocal [2]. Wikipedia states that there is no good evidence that taking citrulline is effective or safe for athletic performance and that it has no confirmed clinical uses [1]. No study in the sources reviewed here has shown that CM increases muscle size.
infobox: Amino acid / organic acid salt (L-citrulline + malic acid)
Dietary supplement; not an approved prescription drug [1]

paras: Citrulline malate is used by lifters and other athletes before training for pump, blood flow and fatigue resistance. T Nation's own pre-workouts list CM among their ingredients, for example a formula containing 6 g of citrulline malate [4][5], and the site describes the compound as reducing lactic acid and ammonia buildup, increasing nitric oxide production and aiding ATP regeneration [3].

Forum members also discuss citrulline alongside erectile dysfunction medication and blood pressure, with some reporting adding citrulline to daily tadalafil or finding it helped their blood pressure [6][7]. Citrulline is also sold as a topical moisturising agent and hair-styling ingredient [1].

A critical review of citrulline malate and exercise performance noted that a single acute 8 g dose has been the most common approach and has produced equivocal results, and attributed the disparity to differing testing protocols, dosing strategy and recently identified quality-control problems with some manufacturers' stated citrulline-to-malate ratios [2].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of foods containing nitrate, polyphenols, arginine or citrulline in endurance performance found no effect for citrulline-rich foods (three studies), while nitrate- and polyphenol-rich foods showed trivial benefits [8]. A systematic review and three-level meta-analysis of citrulline malate and exercise performance has also been published [9]. A 2023 study examined acute L-citrulline on resistance exercise performance and muscle oxygenation in recreationally trained men and women [10].

Wikipedia says there is no good evidence on safety for performance use [1]. Citrulline raises arginine and nitric oxide availability, which is why forum users who take blood pressure or erectile dysfunction drugs ask about interactions [6][7]. A registered trial is testing L-citrulline with tadalafil in mild to moderate erectile dysfunction (NCT07642505) [11]. Disorders of citrulline metabolism, such as adult-onset citrullinemia and the HHH syndrome, are described in the medical literature but concern genetic urea-cycle conditions rather than supplement use [12][13].

Citrulline is converted to arginine, a substrate for nitric oxide synthase; citrulline is released when nitric oxide is made [1]. The performance hypothesis rests on nitric oxide-driven blood flow, improved ammonia homeostasis and malate's possible role in ATP production, none of which the review considered established for performance [2].
The foundation literature on nitric oxide synthesis from L-arginine in vascular endothelium dates to 1988 [14].

The formula of citrulline is H2NC(O)NH(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H [1]. Gastroenterologists described the substance in the late nineteenth century; Japanese researchers Yataro Koga and Ryo Otake isolated it from watermelon in 1914 and it was further characterised in 1930 [1]. Citrullination of proteins is a separate post-translational modification [1].

Exercise: the critical review, the endurance-food meta-analysis and the three-level meta-analysis above [2][8][9], plus a single-blind crossover trial of a multi-ingredient pre-workout (containing citrulline malate, beta-alanine, arginine alpha-ketoglutarate, taurine, tyrosine and caffeine) against caffeine alone on bench press [15]. A registered trial compared L-citrulline and citrulline malate on neuromuscular performance in resistance-trained adults (NCT05183893) [16].

Other populations: trials of L-citrulline in asthma (NCT01715844, NCT02943161), pulmonary hypertension in premature infants (NCT03542812), MELAS (NCT03952234), sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain (NCT06635902), COPD with malnutrition (NCT06212765), preeclampsia in pregnancy, and cold exposure and hypertension (NCT02104375, NCT01462591) are registered or published [17][18][19][20][21][22][23][24][25].

lore.intro: On T Nation citrulline malate appears chiefly as a pre-workout ingredient and in threads about blood pressure and erectile function [4][3][6].
